subject: Private VPC: control-plane / data-plane boundary and egress proofing
messages:
From: Alex Morrison <alex@acme-freight.com>
To: Priya Natarajan <priya@redwood.com>
Cc: markus_klein <markus@redwood.com>, Acme Infra <infra@acme-freight.com>

Subject: Private deployment review — network boundaries and egress proofing

Hi Priya,

Thanks for taking a look at our proposed private deployment topology. We attached a short set of questions (acme-network-questions.pdf) and a high-level diagram. Key asks from our security team: 1) confirm the control-plane to data-plane allowed flows and minimal ports, 2) recommended approach for outbound egress (NAT vs proxy vs private peering), and 3) evidence we can include in our SOC 2 report (audit log locations, KMS/HSM usage).

We’re running the data plane in our us-west-2 VPC, CIDR 10.40.0.0/16, control plane should be in a customer-dedicated subnet behind a managed gateway. We want to keep the data plane strictly private — no direct internet egress except via a company-managed proxy.

Can you and your team validate the diagram and point out any blockers for procurement / security approvals?

Appreciate a brief call if useful — we can do Tuesday afternoon.

Thanks,
Alex
Director of Platform Security
Acme Freight Inc.

Attachments: acme-network-questions.pdf, network-zone-diagram.pdf
From: Priya Natarajan <priya@redwood.com>

Cc: markus_klein <markus@redwood.com>, diego_fernandez <diego@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Private deployment review — network boundaries and egress proofing

Alex — thanks for the clear doc and diagram. High-level answers up front, then details / action items below.

TL;DR: Redwood supports the architecture you outlined. Recommended pattern for private deployments we use is:
- Control plane (management) in a dedicated customer-managed subnet with outbound-only mTLS to Redwood control endpoints (443).
- Data plane nodes in private subnets (no public IPs). Egress from data plane for external integrations goes through a customer-managed egress proxy / NAT with allow-listing.
- All control-plane <-> data-plane comms use a small set of ports and mTLS; we do not require inbound internet to data plane.

Notes/required firewall rules (suggested minimal set):
- Control plane -> Data plane: TCP 443 (mTLS for control API), TCP 8443 (health/metrics scrape, optional), Source: control-plane CIDR, Dest: data-plane node subnets.
- Data plane -> Control plane: TCP 443 (mTLS callbacks/heartbeats) but restricted to destination IPs of the control-plane gateway.
- Data plane -> Egress proxy: TCP 443 (HTTPS) to proxy IPs. No other outbound ports should be allowed.
- KMS/HSM: HTTPS (443) to your KMS endpoints; if you use an on-prem HSM we’ll need IP allow-listing for the control-plane gateway host(s).

We’ll need the following from Acme for a formal diagram and SOC2 artifact generation:
1) Exact control-plane gateway CIDRs / IPs (static if possible)
2) Egress proxy FQDNs/IPs + TLS cert expectations
3) Which audit logs you want reproduced (Redwood can provide request logs, token-level latency/cost logs, and control-plane audit events).

I’ve attached a short checklist (controlplane-egress-checklist.xlsx) and linked a recommended zone diagram. Markus and Diego — please review the port list below and call out any runtime constraints (kernel, kube-proxy, CNI specifics) before I send back a single consolidated doc to Acme.

Thanks,
Priya Natarajan
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Priya / Alex — quick tech notes from infra/runtime side. Agreed with Priya's minimal-rule set. A few practical recommendations to avoid operational pain:

1) Egress strategy: prefer a forced-proxy pattern (customer-managed proxy cluster) rather than NAT gateway in large fleets. Reasons: allows TLS interception for policy, simpler allow-listing, and easier observability. If Acme cannot run a proxy, NAT + explicit route tables are acceptable but you’ll lose fine-grained outbound controls.

2) Ports and protocols: try to keep to HTTPS (443) for control-plane traffic. For internal gRPC TLS we use 8443 on a per-service basis; that can be collapsed into 443 with SNI if you prefer fewer allowed ports. Avoid opening 22 (SSH) into nodes — use a jump host in a dedicated admin subnet.

3) High-availability: have at least two control-plane gateway IPs in separate AZs and add a low-TTL DNS name for the gateway. We recommend health-check ports 8443 allowed from Redwood monitoring IP ranges (we can provide those).

4) KMS/HSM: if Acme has an on-prem HSM, configure the control-plane gateway to talk to it via a dedicated TLS endpoint and add that IP to the control-plane outbound allow-list.

I don’t see anything blocking from a runtime/scale perspective. Diego — any concerns about agent kernel versions or conntrack limits?

-Markus

Redwood Inference

Adding a couple of security/ops guardrails we should include in the final artifact:

- Audit logs: Redwood will expose control-plane audit events (who performed rollout, model version changes, API tokens used). For SOC evidence, we should map these to Acme’s centralized SIEM (they can push via syslog over TLS or S3 delivery).
- Conntrack / ephemeral ports: if you use NAT at scale, watch TCP ephemeral exhaustion — recommend conntrack tuning or using multiple NAT IPs per AZ.
- Agent upgrades: ensure nodes run kernel >= 5.4 and CNI that supports sticky IP masquerade where required; document supported images.
- Egress policy enforcement: enforce allow-listing at the proxy and also at the route-table level (defense in depth).

I’m attaching a short checklist (controlplane-egress-checklist.xlsx) with the items we’ll capture in the final deliverable. Once Acme provides the gateway IPs and proxy FQDNs we can produce a signed architecture diagram and a SOC2-facing Evidence table.

Diego
